lockedSlides.title: Where to Start: The Three Questions
lockedSlides.sub: Before you touch a wall, answer three questions. They decide your order of work, your budget, and whether you keep the house's soul.

bullets.d: Leaks, gutters, grading, damp basement. Water is the only enemy that can undo every other repair. If the answer is 'not sure', Chapter 1's audit is where you start.
Age and type of wiring, plumbing, heating. Old systems are safety and insurability issues — they get done before walls close, and they set your budget floor.
List the features you bought the house for: plaster walls, windows, doors, built-ins, floors. Everything you'd hate to lose becomes a 'restore, don't replace' item in Chapter 4.
Whatever your total budget, hold back 20% as a surprise reserve. Old houses WILL produce one — this column is the difference between a pause and a panic.
Before committing to a whole-house plan, finish one small room end-to-end. You'll learn the house's rhythm, your contractor's reliability, and your real cost per square foot.

notes: Answer these three questions on the first page of a notebook — then everything else in this Kit hangs off them.
If you can only buy one tool this month, buy a moisture meter (~$30). It answers Q1 for every room in ten seconds.

lockedSlides.title: Part I — Exterior & Systems
lockedSlides.sub: The timed room-by-room walkthrough that tells you what you're really dealing with. First six checks — exterior, structure and concealed systems.

bullets.d: Ask for the roof permit date; 20+ years with 2+ layers = $8k-$18k replacement. Check gutters for debris and grading that drains toward the house.
Hairline cracks are fine. Stair-step cracks in masonry, bowing walls, or doors that won't close = structural engineer ($400-$800) before you negotiate anything.
Roll a marble across each room. Deep sags can mean cut joists or failed beams — a $3k-$15k repair.
Cracked but stable is repairable ($2-$6/sq ft). Loose, bowing plaster with failed keys needs reattachment or replacement ($5-$12/sq ft).
Look for knob-and-tube (porcelain knobs in attic/basement) and any panel older than 1980. Full rewire on 1,800 sq ft runs $8k-$20k.
Galvanized steel = 40-70 year lifespan, often rusted shut. Repipe runs $4k-$12k. Check for a sewer-camera line if you can.

notes: Every major finding above is a price-reduction lever. Negotiate with this list, not emotions.

lockedSlides.title: Part II — Windows, Hazards & Paperwork
lockedSlides.sub: The last six checks, plus the two phone calls that protect you at the closing table.

bullets.d: Original wood windows are worth restoring ($200-$600 each, DIY) vs $800-$1,200 each replaced. Count every one — it adds up fast.
Pre-1978 houses likely have lead paint; test ($50-$400). Encapsulation is legal and cheaper than removal. Asbestos test on old flooring/insulation: $40-$150 per sample.
Old houses often have 2-4 inches. Adding to R-38 runs $1.5-$3.5/sq ft and pays back fast on heating bills.
HVAC 15+ years = $6k-$12k replacement; water heater 10+ = $900-$2,000. Both are negotiation levers.
Call the building department: open permits, un-permitted additions, or historic-district restrictions. Historic districts can control windows and exterior colors.
Kitchen/bath updates: were they permitted? Un-permitted work becomes YOUR problem at resale — document everything.

notes: Not handy? Budget $1,500-$3,000 for a licensed GC's walkthrough estimate before closing.
This chapter is free on the site — the paid Kit adds the cost columns, budget math and the sequence that follows it.

lockedSlides.title: The Five Budget Rules
lockedSlides.sub: These five rules protect the down payment better than any spreadsheet formula.

bullets.d: Take 20% of total budget off the top into a separate account. It's not 'money for extras' — it's the old-house tax. When it's untouched at the end, celebrate.
Line items beat lump sums. You need to compare and to cut scope later without renegotiating everything.
Progress payments tied to completed milestones, 10% held until final inspection and punch list.
Water, structure, electrical, plumbing, heat — price these first. If they eat the budget, the wants wait. That's not failure, that's order.

bullets.t: DIY the finish, hire the systems
bullets.d: Paint, trim, hardware, floors (with rentals) are DIY-able. Electrical, plumbing, structure are not — hire licensed pros.

notes: The 20% reserve is the column most spreadsheets are missing. Build it first — always.

lockedSlides.title: Days 1-30 — Secure, Inspect, Stop the Water
lockedSlides.sub: The #1 old-house money-waster is doing work out of order. This sequence protects you from ripping out last month's work. Days are working days.

bullets.d: Change locks, turn off water if leaving it, photograph EVERY room and wall before touching anything. These photos win insurance and contractor disputes.
Structural engineer (if flagged), sewer line camera ($300-$500), asbestos and lead tests. Cheap now, catastrophic to skip.
Roof, gutters, downspouts, grading. Water is the only enemy that can undo every other repair — fix these before any interior work.
Electrical rewire and plumbing repipe before walls close. This is the messy demo phase — by the book, with permits.
Foundation repairs, joist sistering, insulation. Window restoration happens now too (from inside or after exterior work).

notes: Water → systems → structure → walls → floors. Old houses reward this order every single time.

lockedSlides.title: Days 30-90 — Walls, Paint, Floors, Trim
lockedSlides.sub: The finish phase. Each step protects the one before it — do them in exactly this order.

bullets.d: Plaster repair or drywall. The messiest phase — do it before floors and trim, never after.
Prime first (especially stained old plaster), then two finish coats. Paint is the cheapest thing that transforms an old house — spend time here, not money.
Refinish hardwood after painting — sanding dust ruins fresh paint. $3-$5/sq ft professionally, $1.5-$2.5/sq ft DIY with rentals.
Restore original trim and doors — sanding + paint/stain + new hardware costs ~20% of replacing. This is where the character comes back.
Period lighting, switch plates, towel bars, and the walk-through punch list. Celebrate with the one-room test from Chapter 1.

notes: The 20% reserve lives here: sequence slippage is normal, panic is not.
If a contractor wants to 'just do the kitchen first' — ask them to read this chapter's order of operations.

lockedSlides.title: Keep the Bones
lockedSlides.sub: The features you bought the house for are assets, not liabilities. Restore them — never replace them.

bullets.t: Keep: original plaster, windows, doors, floors
bullets.d: These are the bones. Restore them (Chapters 3-4 cover the order). New drywall and replacement windows read as 'flipped' — and cost more.
Original wood doors, radiators, cast-iron tubs (if intact), stained glass, built-ins — always restore these. Replacement is both pricier and lesser.

bullets.t: Add: one statement piece per room
bullets.d: A teak credenza in the living room, a cane chair in the corner, a terrazzo bath vanity. One period anchor per room, never a museum.
First impressions sell the whole house to visitors (and to you). A restored front door, a period mat, one warm light, one framed print — done.

notes: When in doubt, walk the room and ask: what did the original owners do here? Then do that, better, with better light.

lockedSlides.title: Style the Skin
lockedSlides.sub: Warm woods, honest materials, one or two bold accents — the whole recipe for an old house that feels composed, not decorated.

bullets.d: 70% warm cream & wood tones, 25% a deep accent (olive, terracotta, navy), 5% brass or ochre detail. This is how period rooms feel composed, not decorated.
The fastest character upgrade in an old house: sunburst clocks, brass sconces, globe pendants. $60-$200 per fixture changes a room overnight.
Restore the frames, then hang simple linen curtains on brass rods — full height, mounted high. It makes ceilings feel taller and rooms feel softer.
New cabinet faces, counters, appliances and hardware on the existing footprint beats a full gut — 40-60% less money, same daily joy.
Keep the footprint, add terrazzo-look tile, brass fixtures, a period mirror. Old-house bathrooms feel 'of their time' without a remodel price tag.

notes: Mid-century style is not a style you impose — it's the era that loved old houses. Warm woods + honest materials + one or two bold accents is the whole recipe.

lockedSlides.title: Six Hunting Grounds
lockedSlides.sub: Where to find the right stuff for an old house — and why you buy FIRST, because period pieces disappear fast.

bullets.d: Original doors, radiators, hardware, lighting at 30-60% of new. Plan a Saturday trip — and buy first, because period pieces disappear fast.
House of Antique Hardware, Van Dyke's — knobs, hinges, switch plates that match the house's era.
US Heritage Group, LimeWorks.us for authentic lime repair; Big Wally's Plaster Magic for reattaching loose plaster without full replacement.
Glazing compound (Sarco Type M), sash cord, brass hardware — a full window set runs $150-$400 in materials vs $1,000+ replacement.
Old-fashioned milk paint (The Real Milk Paint Co.) for authentic color on woodwork; ask the lumber yard about 'period profile' millwork for trim.
Facebook Marketplace and estate sales are goldmines for period bathroom tile, clawfoot tubs and built-in hardware.

notes: Buy salvage first, store it safely before demo starts. The perfect clawfoot tub will not wait for your schedule.

lockedSlides.title: Room Priority — Where Money Goes First
lockedSlides.sub: The room order that protects both livability and value when money is tight.

bullets.d: Roof, structure, electrical, plumbing, heating — non-negotiable and first. Everything else waits.
The rooms that end daily pain and sell a house. Footprint-first refreshes, never full guts.
Primary bedroom, living room and entry — paint, floors and light after systems are done. Character restoration here pays in daily enjoyment and resale.
Guest rooms and basement are cosmetic, low-pressure, perfect for DIY weekends. Curb appeal last, once the house works (grading away from the foundation excepted — do that early).

notes: Priority rule: anything that keeps water out, power on or heat in beats anything that looks nice.

lockedSlides.title: Ten Interview Questions (1-5)
lockedSlides.sub: Ten questions that separate old-house pros from generalists learning on your dime. Ask them before you sign anything.

bullets.t: "How many pre-1950 houses have you worked on?"
bullets.d: The right answer is 'several, recently' with names. Old houses are a specialty, not a sideline.
The right answer involves lime plaster, plaster washers, or experienced plasterers — not just 'we'll drywall over it.'
They should, include it in the bid, and know your local historic-district rules.
Removal or a licensed electrician's evaluation — never 'leave it, it's fine.'
Line items beat lump sums. You need to compare and cut scope later without renegotiating everything.

notes: Always get three bids — not the cheapest, the one who answers these questions best at a fair price.

lockedSlides.title: Questions 6-10 & the 13 Pitfalls
lockedSlides.sub: The second half of the interview — plus the mistakes that break new owners (and how the change-order process protects you).

bullets.d: Written, signed, before work starts. Old houses WILL produce changes; the process is what protects you.

bullets.t: "Who are the subs — licensed and insured?"
bullets.d: Electricians, plumbers, structural work must be licensed. Verify insurance covers the site.
Never more than 10-15% down, progress payments tied to milestones, 10% held until final inspection and punch list.

bullets.t: "Can I see three old-house projects you've finished?"
bullets.d: Go see them. Photos are marketing; standing in the house is truth.

bullets.t: "What surprises have you found in houses like mine?"
bullets.d: If they can't name 2-3, they haven't done this before. Their answers tell you what contingency to budget.

1) No surprise reserve. 2) Work out of order. 3) Gutting instead of restoring. 4) Replacing windows instead of restoring. 5) Skipping permits. 6) Drywalling over plaster. 7) Painting before priming. 8) Floors before painting. 9) Cheapest bid. 10) No change-order process. 11) Ignoring grading/water. 12) Buying new when salvage exists. 13) Forgetting the 20% tax.

notes: This chapter alone has saved owners more than the Kit's price in change-order fees.

disclaimer: Ranges reflect typical US market conditions (2025-2026) and vary by region. Always get three contractor bids, a structural inspection, and a local code check before starting. This kit is educational planning guidance, not engineering advice.
